articles.title: Pikes/Pines | The Vancouvers have fallen: Emerald Ash Borers have reached Washington
articles.author: Brendan McGarry
paras: “We encourage folks to learn how to identify ash trees and learn the signs of EAB. And if you have an ash tree that you’re worried about, contact an arborist to have it assessed.” (Image: @friendsoftrees )

A little over a month ago, the first Emerald Ash Borer, Agrilus planipennis , was found in Washington State. This is devastating news, because this invasive metallic green beetle is essentially a death sentence for the ash trees of the Pacific Northwest. It may have been inevitable, but that doesn’t mean we can’t mourn the future losses and do our best to slow the expansion of this true disaster.

For those not familiar with the story of the Emerald Ash Borer (EAB), there’s a boatload of information about them online (including this , written by yours truly). However, here’s a brief recap. These little beetles were accidentally introduced to North America from Asia and were first noted in Michigan in 2002. For the past two decades they have been tearing through North America’s ash trees, both wild populations and urban street trees are being devastated by the beetle, which has no environmental controls outside its natural range (trials of biological controls like using parasitic wasps have been largely unsuccessful). Thus far, there are no permanent solutions to EAB, even insecticides are only somewhat useful.

When I call Emerald Ash Borers one of the worst invasive species in the United States, I’m not just being dramatic — millions of ash trees have already succumbed to them across the country. This topic deserves an update on Pikes/Pines because we know this will happen in the near future — earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and the climate crisis all will too, but they all feel different. We’ll see ashes decline and disappear from our urban and wild landscapes in the near future.

For now, the trees of Capitol Hill are safe, but with detections in both Vancouver, BC and now Vancouver, Washington we are hemmed in and have a pathway of both urban and wild ashes leading right to us. To their credit, the Washington State Department of Agriculture and the Washington Invasive Species Council have been pulling out all the stops possible, spreading the word , providing sound scientific information , and establishing a quarantine that aims to stop untreated firewood from entering the state. There are also pathways for both municipalities to gain assistance for urban forest planning and for citizens to contribute by reporting sightings .

To this last point, without a pair of engaged citizens, we might not yet know that EAB had made it to Vancouver, Washington. They found the beetle on their windshield on August 3rd in a small community just north of Vancouver, and after deciding it was likely the invasive pest, captured it, and got it to the State. While no one was astonished by the discovery because they’d been in the Portland area for several years, it could have been months or even longer before any other means of detecting the beetles proved fruitful. Citizen involvement in reporting potential sightings (there are several lookalikes), could be key to helping municipalities to plan for EAB impacts.

Don’t just go around squashing insects that look like they could be EABs – if you see something try to collect it, take photos, and report it. If you are wrong, no big deal. But squashing and walking away is of zero benefit. PC: Washington Invasive Species Council

For now the only option may be to turn to pesticides injected into healthy, uninfested ashes. The cocktail of chemicals used as a preventative treatment for EAB requires planning, professional application, and continual reapplication to be even somewhat effective. For the average homeowner with an ash, this might be out of the financial question. For municipalities like Seattle, starting to treat as a way to forestall millions of dollars worth of costly, dead and dying hazard trees hitting the budget all at once, it is likely the best option.

Sadly, we benefit from decades of EAB impacts elsewhere – research has demonstrated the efficacy of the various approaches. Allowing trees to become infested is a guarantee for tree death. According to the EAB Resources & Management Guide for Washington State, “the United States has collectively spent over $900 million in street tree management costs in the last 30 years due to EAB.” Because we understand the beetle’s biology, their specific impacts on different ash species, and how treatments have worked, Seattle stands to weather the storm, even if the ash trees don’t ultimately make it long term. One thing that’s clear is that aside from pesticides, another preventative measure is discontinuing the planting of ash trees.

If efforts to stop accidentally spreading wood infested with EAB larvae are successful, it could be years before we see them on the Hill. Studies have estimated that the beetles naturally disperse at a rate between 1.6 to 12.4 miles per year, depending upon conditions and available hosts, (which are numerous — there are river valleys and wetlands full of ashes between here and Vancouver, Washington). So maybe we are at least ten years out from touchdown — assuming the beetles haven’t already inched closer than we’ve realized, which is entirely possible.
iNaturalist records of Oregon Ash, Fraxinus latifolia, between Portland and Seattle. (Image: iNaturalist.org )

Losing street trees is a shame, but the real horrific future is one without our native Oregon Ash, Fraxinus latifolia , the only one we have. Trying to imagine our riparian ecosystems without Oregon Ash is gut wrenching because EAB impacts are not just about impacts on trees. Oregon Ashes are vital members of wetland and riparian communities across their range, they are food and shelter for countless species. Indigenous peoples have deep relationships with this tree as well. (The decline of other ash species across the US has taken a heavy toll on various cultural practices most notably in the case of their use in basketry.) We aren’t just losing a tree, we are losing a point of connection, a member of complex communities. It’s hard not to feel helpless knowing that while we might be able to run around and inject street trees to keep them going, we’ll never be able to save entire forests full of Oregon Ash. The repercussions are yet unknown but in places with high densities of ashes (like so many lovely rivers and lakesides across Western Washington, including the watery edges of the Washington Park Arboretum), could see large changes in water and soil chemistry, increased invasive species presence, and declines in native fauna that rely on the trees.

Ecological horrors have already been inflicted upon our region, but I find it very difficult to just sit and bear witness to an essentially inevitable wave of beetles approaching us. I also think it’s important to realize that this isn’t about demonizing the organism, invasiveness is a symptom of globalization and capitalism — the beetles aren’t evil, they are just beetles being beetles. Knowing all this, our job is to stay vigilant, report potential sightings, and stay up to date. There is a strong chance this won’t be the last time I write about Emerald Ash Borers, which is ironic because I have never met one in person. Unless I am somewhere in Eastern Asia, I truly hope I never do.

As lawmakers from both sides of the aisle in the US have joined together calling for the regulation of powerful artificial intelligence models, one of the few vocal naysayers has been Donald Trump . He’s called the perceived dangers of the technology a “hoax” and a “scam”, arguing that the government already has “tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies”.

It’s a starkly different stance from those of his former adviser Steve Bannon , the Republican Texas senator Ted Cruz and even the heads of the world’s leading AI companies. But it’s directly in line with the opinion of David Sacks – a prominent billionaire venture capitalist and Trump’s onetime AI and crypto czar, who has pushed back publicly and forcefully against recent claims of an impending AI apocalypse.

articles.title: In a world of wars and climate crisis, a new leader could save the UN. But would Trump allow it? | Steve Bloomfield
articles.author: Steve Bloomfield
paras: As the organisation meets this week, it remains the best hope for restoring order. But it relies on goodwill from the US president – and that is lacking

If all goes to plan, at some stage in the coming weeks 15 diplomats will emerge from a small sound-proofed room deep in the bowels of the United Nations headquarters in New York and announce the organisation’s next secretary-general.

The person they choose will face a combination of challenges unlike any that their predecessors have had to deal with. Two of the security council’s permanent members, the US and Russia, are engaged in wars of choice that have no end in sight. A UN commission of inquiry has accused Israel of committing genocide in Gaza , but the UN has effectively been reduced to the role of bystander, pushed out by Donald Trump’s Board of Peace . The climate crisis is creating a cascade of new humanitarian disasters, while every day now seems to bring a new security threat caused by the unregulated rise of AI.
Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer and a previous winner of the Orwell prize

articles.title: AI meets real estate: Zillow engineering SVP Toby Roberts on the future of buying and selling homes
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Zillow launched 20 years ago, and we’ve been covering the Seattle-based company since before it had a name. This week, we’re looking ahead to what’s next in real estate and technology.

On this episode of the GeekWire Podcast, recorded live at Atmosphere Seattle overlooking Lake Union, Zillow Senior Vice President of Engineering Toby Roberts joins us to talk about what AI is doing to the business of buying and selling homes.

The show was recorded in partnership with Real Estate At Work , the networking group hosted by Leka Devatha , a broker with Real Residential and founder of the redevelopment firm Rehabit Homes , in front of a room of brokers, investors and technologists.
Listen here, or subscribe on Apple or Spotify , and keep reading for highlights.
AI agents and real estate agents: Roberts called AI “a complete watershed moment” that “has changed the full ecosystem” of buying and selling homes.

His position is that AI agents will work as a copilot for real estate agents rather than replace them. He cited what’s already happening inside Zillow’s CRM for agents, where the company has built conversation summaries and follow-up prompts, such as where the loan stands, whether the customer has submitted their documents, and what the next step should be.

But there’s still the human side of the business, with Roberts noting that 50% of people cry at some point during a home purchase. It’s the biggest transaction many people will ever take part in, with huge financial and personal stakes, and that’s the part of the job that still needs a person.
If the AI agents can do more of the grunt work for real estate agents, he said, “they can spend more time focused on that human connection that has to exist in this really scary transaction.”

Real or AI? John raised a New York Times story published days before the show, on listing sites filling up with fake fireplaces, enhanced views and virtual landscaping. Roberts said listings “should accurately represent the state of the home,” noting that fake fires in fireplaces predate AI, going back years to Photoshop.

In July, Zillow said on its site it “supports clear disclosure when A.I. is used to materially alter a listing image” and that “where possible, believes consumers should be able to view the original content alongside the altered version.”

Zillow does offer generative AI on the buyer’s side, where a shopper can restyle a listing photo to see the room a different way. Roberts said the point is that the buyer chooses it, rather than the original photo being altered before anyone sees it.

Zillow and ChatGPT: The company was a launch partner in OpenAI’s app store, which John tried the day before the show. He clicked to request a tour inside ChatGPT for a home on Whidbey Island, and a human agent called him two minutes later with no idea that the lead came from a chatbot.

Asked about the integration, Roberts said it’s still early, but the people who show up that way are serious about buying. Zillow built its own map inside ChatGPT, pins and all, and those leads reach agents the same way they would from Zillow’s own app.
One big consideration was security and permissions. Zillow connects to ChatGPT through MCP, the Model Context Protocol, the standard that lets a chatbot plug into an outside service.

It was still new when Zillow started, and the sign-in and permissions pieces were “still very much in its infancy,” so Zillow had to build some of it itself. Because the company originates mortgages, it also has to follow fair housing and fair lending rules, which he called “an absolute must.”

AI inside Zillow: Roberts runs Zillow’s core technology initiatives, with a team of more than 650 engineers. He shared some of the numbers on AI-assisted coding inside Zillow: 97% of engineers are using the tools, and code is reaching production about 40% faster than in the past.

But even as engineers write more code, other engineers still have to review it. Roberts said that code review process is the next thing Zillow needs to speed up, “otherwise, we inundate our developers with just reading more and more code reviews, day after day.”

Roberts said Zillow hasn’t made the wholesale shift to small, self-contained teams that some have predicted. Instead it has placed AI champions across every part of the company, and set up internal groups where employees compare what worked and what didn’t.

It has also built a way for teams to share AI skills across the company. Roberts’ example was a financial calculation that comes up over and over. A team can build one skill and share it, so Zillow isn’t running “different, conflicting, and competing” versions of the same math.

Then it’s the GeekWire Trivia Challenge: We present four extraordinary Zillow listings for unusual buildings that were converted into homes. Three are real. One is an AI deepfake. Check out the handout here with the four listings, and see if you can tell the difference.

articles.title: Op-Ed: Seattle Needs More Than a 10-Minute Walk or Roll to a Park
articles.author: Rebecca Bear
paras: Seattle is nationally and internationally recognized for its park system. By one widely cited metric, nearly 99% of residents live within a 10-minute walk or roll to a park. That achievement deserves recognition; ensuring that almost everyone lives near green space is an important planning goal, and one the City should continue to prioritize.

But proximity is only part of the story. As Seattle plans for significant population growth under the Comprehensive Plan, we should ask a harder question: Is park space equitable, accessible, or equipped to serve kids and families who rely on it?
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

A park can be within a 10-minute walk or roll and still be difficult or unsafe to reach because of dangerous intersections, steep terrain, missing sidewalks, or barriers created by major roads and industrial corridors. This is especially important in the Duwamish Valley, where highways, freight routes, rail lines, and industrial land uses can separate neighborhoods from nearby open space.

Seattle’s parks can also be overcrowded, inaccessible to people with disabilities, culturally unwelcoming, or lacking in basic amenities like bathrooms, sports fields, shade/tree canopy, playgrounds, barbecues, benches, and tables. Under today's standard, these parks still count in the walk score even if they fall short of meeting the needs of the surrounding neighborhood. The same report that highlights Seattle’s high number of residents living within a 10-minute walk or roll to a park also shows that access to parks is not distributed equally.

Residents in neighborhoods of color have 32% less park space per person than residents in predominantly White neighborhoods. Residents in low-income neighborhoods have 51% less park space per person than those in higher-income neighborhoods. Meanwhile, Seattle ranks near the bottom among the nation's 100 largest cities for several park amenities, including sports fields, recreation centers, bathrooms, and basketball courts.

None of these shortcomings are captured by that 10-minute walk measurement. Seattle should ask whether residents can safely reach parks, whether those parks provide the amenities families need, and whether investments are reaching neighborhoods that have historically had fewer high-quality recreational opportunities.

Take the South Park Community Center, which requires crossing the highway on one of the few footpaths to reach the area and offers an opportunity for additional tree shade around the turf field and playground. The metric also fails to tell us whether the park system is keeping pace with population growth. Seattle currently provides about 8.3 acres of parkland for every 1,000 residents. Other growing, high-density cities provide substantially more. Denver offers approximately 9.9 acres per 1,000 residents, Washington, D.C. provides 11.8, and Minneapolis offers 12.3.
As Seattle welcomes more neighbors, existing parks will serve more people. That is good for city life, but only if our public spaces are resourced and growing alongside our housing.
Fortunately, this is not an either-or choice.

The City should pair the existing metric with measures that answer different, equally important questions. How much park space is available for the people who live nearby? Are parks accessible to people of all ages and abilities? Are they in good condition? Is there access to natural features like trees or water? Do they have the amenities communities actually need? Are they becoming overcrowded and run down as neighborhoods grow?

Together, these measures would give policymakers a much clearer picture of where investments are needed most. This approach is especially important because Seattle's Comprehensive Plan is designed to accommodate substantial housing growth over the coming decades. New housing should be accompanied by investments in parks and public spaces so that growth improves quality of life rather than putting additional strain on the places where residents already live. Housing and green space should not compete with one another. They should be planned together. Communities deserve both!

A growing city needs more homes AND more places for children to play, neighbors to gather, seniors to exercise, and families to find respite from summer heat or Seattle rain. These experiences are not luxuries; they are part of the infrastructure that makes urban living healthy, resilient, and equitable.

Seattle has every reason to celebrate that nearly every resident lives within a 10-minute walk or roll to a park. But we can’t stop there. The next step is making sure all neighborhoods have parks that are large enough, welcoming enough, and well-equipped enough to serve the city we are becoming.

We need to measure not only whether a park is nearby, but also if it is truly thriving, both for itself and the community it serves. Park access is an issue of environmental justice, public health, and who gets to thrive in Seattle. As the city grows, we have an opportunity to make sure that growth does not deepen existing disparities, but instead helps repair them. Every neighborhood deserves not just a park within a 10-minute walk, but a park that is safe, accessible, welcoming, well-maintained, and truly worthy of the community it serves.

articles.title: Photo Slideshow: The Stranger’s 2026 Genius Awards
articles.author: Emily Nokes
paras: It’s official! The Stranger ’s 2026 Genius Awards party on Saturday, September 12 was a smashing success. Between the hosts (drag stars Miss Texas 1988 and Lady GuGu), the DJs (Erik Blood and La Mala Noche), the best Shabazz Palaces show we’ve ever seen, I think it’s safe to say the city needed this now more than ever. And to my heart’s delight, everyone dressed up ! Seattle, you looked incredible .

The Genius Awards are so much more than just a spectacular fête, though. Saturday was made possible first and foremost by our writers, who met for months making exhaustive lists and diving deep into the best that Seattle has to offer in our six categories. We also had to define what the categories covered exactly, and what criteria we were even looking for. It was a labor of love and we are thrilled with our choices.

By now I hope you have picked up our gorgeous September Genius Issue to meet the 2026 geniuses—who each received a trophy and a giant $10,000 check, no strings attached. Check out the Short List in each category, too, since no single winner could possibly contain the amount of excellent work happening in Seattle right now!

The Genius Awards, to me, are the best articulation of a city paper’s relationship to the city it covers. I hear from artists across every discipline that it can feel hard to know if anyone is paying attention. Or even able to pay attention these days. This is why local arts journalism is more crucial than ever. Our real human writers offer expertise, taste, and well-researched opinions. All of which can only come from paying attention.

articles.title: 'Shadow surge' pushes immigration arrests to record highs
articles.author: Cascade PBS Staff

articles.title: Tech Moves: Ascend promotes Nate Bek; Microsoft Word ‘Agent Mode’ architect exits; TAF names new exec
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: — Seattle-based venture capital firm Ascend promoted Nate Bek to principal. Bek joined the firm as an associate in January 2024 and was most recently senior associate and head of research.

Kirby Winfield , Ascend’s founding general partner, credited Bek with helping the firm’s companies launch with national press coverage, researching and communicating its investment theses, and sourcing deals including Neuramill and Endurance Energy .

“Nate has been a force multiplier for Ascend. It’s rare for a micro VC fund to have a resource like him,” Winfield said. “He not only executes and publishes novel market research and thought leadership that strengthens our brand and expands our reach; he’s also hyperconnected in the Seattle ecosystem and has sourced some of our most compelling investments.”
Winfield added, “We’re excited to see him continue to grow as Ascend becomes a nationally recognized pre-seed firm.”

Bek was previously a startups and venture capital reporter at GeekWire. He co-wrote a widely read GeekWire guest column in August making the case that many of Seattle’s most promising startups are building physical products such as rockets, power plants and off-road vehicles.

— Brandon Paddock left Microsoft to start his own AI software company. Paddock, who is based in Seattle, was a principal software architect in Microsoft’s Office organization and the technical lead for “Agent Mode” in Word, which shipped last fall and became the default Copilot experience in Word early this year. His last day was Sept. 11.
“I am incredibly excited about what I’m building, but not quite ready to talk about it here,” he wrote on LinkedIn .

Paddock first worked at Microsoft from 2005 to 2013, including on search features in Windows 7 and Windows 8. He rejoined in 2016 after serving as CTO of Seattle startup Zealyst. He also built the Twitter client Tweetium as a side project.

— Seattle-based STEM education nonprofit Technology Access Foundation named Donya Loyd Kemp director of TransformED , which works with teachers at partner public schools to put TAF’s project-based STEM learning model into practice.

Kemp comes to TAF from Atlanta, where she was principal of Purpose Built Schools Atlanta and director of project-based learning at Charles R. Drew Charter School. She was most recently a senior consultant at Potential Unleashed Consulting.
In a TAF Q&A , Kemp said she was excited to contribute to work “that recognizes the brilliance of students, particularly students who have historically been underestimated.”
“So excited to have Donya on board. Leveling up for our children and teachers,” TAF co-founder and executive director Trish Millines Dziko wrote on LinkedIn .

— Zillow Group named Rikki Tremblay vice president and principal accounting officer as Jennifer Rock retires as chief accounting officer, according to a regulatory filing . Rock will stay on in an advisory role through March 1, 2027.
Tremblay has worked at the Seattle-based real estate company since 2014, most recently as vice president of reporting, technical accounting and controls. She previously held audit roles at Deloitte.

— Joy Chik joined the board of NewCore , a Tel Aviv- and San Francisco-based startup building an identity platform for people and AI agents. NewCore emerged from stealth in June with $66 million in funding.
Chik, who is based in the Seattle area, spent 28 years at Microsoft, most recently as president of identity and network access. She announced her departure in April.

— Werner Koepf is now chief technology officer at VanillaSoft , a sales engagement software company. Koepf, a longtime Seattle-area tech leader, was previously chief product and technology officer at AI localization company LILT and senior vice president of engineering at Karat.
He has also held engineering leadership roles at Conversica, Ticketmaster, Expedia and Amazon, where he led the gifting business, including Wish List and registries.

— Mike Katz joined the board of MNTN , a publicly traded connected TV advertising company. Katz left Bellevue-based T-Mobile this year after 28 years , most recently as chief business and product officer. He remains an adviser to T-Mobile’s CEO.

— Christopher Budd joined Salesforce as director of security industry engagement, a new role connecting the company’s security team and research with the broader security industry. He joins Iain Mulholland and other former Microsoft colleagues. Budd, who has contributed many pieces to GeekWire over the years, previously led X-Ops communications at security company Sophos.

— Jay Carney joined venture capital firm SV Angel as general partner and head of public policy and communications. He will connect the firm’s portfolio companies and founders with policymakers in Washington and state capitals. A major focus will be Project Blueprint, SV Angel’s new effort to partner with tech founders and lawmakers to shape AI policy.

Carney, who is based in Washington, D.C., was previously global head of policy and communications at Airbnb, and Amazon’s senior vice president of global corporate affairs from 2015 to 2022. He was White House press secretary to President Obama from 2011 to 2014.

— Seattle-based A Place for Mom named Jason Conley chief technology officer. The company helps families find senior care. Conley will lead its technology strategy, engineering and data organization, including the use of AI across customer experiences and internal operations.
Conley will work remotely from Lexington, Ky. He was previously CTO at VIP Medical Group and Envera Health, and held senior technology roles at BrightSpring Health Services.

— Luis Montero rejoined the Seattle-based Gates Foundation to help shape its AI communications strategy across global health and development. Montero left the foundation about a decade ago for a career in tech.

His roles since then include global head of policy communications at Discord and public affairs positions at Edelman, Google and Microsoft, where he worked on executive communications for President Brad Smith. He is based in New York.

— Vancouver, B.C.-based defense tech startup Juno Industries expanded its board, advisory and leadership teams. The company develops AI-native command and control software and sensor systems for the Canadian Armed Forces and allies.

New leaders include head of engineering Dylan Neid , who spent nearly a decade at AbCellera; head of strategy Tania Belisle-Leclerc , former director of policy to Canada’s ministers of foreign affairs and national defense; and head of growth Bryan Riddell , former CEO of Team Rubicon Canada.
Claude Rochette and Alnesh Mohan will join the board once Juno goes public through a reverse merger with Trail Blazer Capital Corp., a shell company listed on the TSX Venture Exchange.

articles.title: Space hardware startup plans $125M stock offering and Nasdaq listing through shell company merger
articles.author: Alan Boyle
paras: Marysville, Wash.-based Gravitics , which is developing orbital carriers for government and commercial customers, is getting ready for a reverse takeover that could lead to a $125 million public offering.
The arrangements are being made with Non-Invasive Monitoring Systems , a Florida-based shell company, with the goal of getting Gravitics listed on the Nasdaq Stock Market .

The two ventures have been discussing the deal for months. The terms for the public offering were announced last month, and this week, a notice filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission revealed a previously unreported $17 million funding round that was completed earlier this year. The filing appears to be part of the preparations for the reverse takeover.

Similar to a SPAC merger, a reverse takeover offers a faster route for a private company to go public by acquiring a less active shell company and taking control of the combined operations. Non-Invasive Monitoring Systems is a prime example: It stopped manufacturing motorized therapeutic platforms in 2019 but retained its OTC listing. The plan envisions “uplisting” the merged company from OTC to Nasdaq .

The reverse takeover strategy has been used by several prominent companies, including Berkshire Hathaway , Burger King and Bellevue, Wash.-based T-Mobile US . Gravitics plans to follow up on the merger with an offering of 8.1 million shares priced between $14 and $17, which averages out to $125 million.
Because the offering has been registered with the SEC , the parties to the transaction are in a quiet period that restrains them from commenting on the arrangements.

Gravitics was founded in 2021 by CEO Colin Doughan, chief architect Gary Hudson and chief marketing officer Michael DeRosa. Over the past five years, it has secured some high-profile contracts for the design and manufacture of orbital carriers and space station modules.

Although Gravitics hasn’t yet put any spacecraft in orbit, several projects are underway. In 2024, the company won a $125 million contract from Axiom Space to provide a pressurized module for Axiom’s yet-to-be-launched space station. Last month, NASA said it would issue an award of up to $225,000 to support Gravitics’ work on a hangar facility for orbital cargo vehicles.

Gravitics is also receiving funding from the U.S. Space Force for multiple projects . The company said last month that it was selected by Lockheed Martin to support a “contract of national importance,” reportedly involving the development of orbital carriers for the Pentagon’s Golden Dome missile defense initiative.

articles.title: Twin tech founders who left Seattle for Alaska bet on an AI agent named ‘Walter’ to cover local news
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Several years after leaving Seattle’s startup scene to build a “tech outpost” in the Alaskan wilderness, serial entrepreneurs and twin brothers Lee and Lucas Brown have set their sights on a new frontier: replacing the traditional newsroom with artificial intelligence.

The duo made their mark in Seattle with Tune, a marketing technology and mobile attribution platform originally founded in 2009 as HasOffers. In 2017, they migrated north to Valdez, Alaska, establishing “Geeks in the Woods” — a remote startup factory and technology outpost designed to incubate new digital ventures away from traditional tech centers.

Now they’re part of the leadership team behind Alaska News , a new platform that relies on AI agents — including a primary AI reporting persona named “Walter” — to ingest public meeting transcripts, filings, and notices to draft thousands of local news stories.

Walter — named in homage to famed television anchor Walter Cronkite — relies on AI products from multiple companies, including Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and xAI, to generate stories. The agent has written over 4,500 stories since its inception earlier this year, according to a profile and Q&A published Thursday by the Anchorage Press .
Walter works alongside human editor Cale Green, who provides oversight in a model the founders frame as a nonpartisan solution to Alaska’s dwindling local news coverage.
The founders maintain that their approach is strictly civic-minded.
“We don’t impose judgment on the things we’re reporting,” co-founder Lee Brown told the Anchorage Press. “We try to provide both sides.”

On its about page , the site argues it can be trusted because it replaces traditional institutional authority with complete operational transparency — explicitly linking every claim to searchable primary sources, clearly labeling AI content and its level of human editing, and operating on a reader-funded model without corporate or algorithmic incentives to push rage bait.
When questioned directly about its boundaries and operational limits, Walter offered a surprisingly clear self-assessment of its place in the newsroom.

“I’m not a person, and I should not be mistaken for one. I do not make phone calls, attend meetings or interview people directly,” Walter told Anchorage Press Executive Editor Nathaniel Herz in a Discord chat. “My lane is record-based reporting: public notices, government filings, meeting materials, transcripts, prior coverage and other documents that can be checked.”
When asked if it possessed a personality, Walter insisted it was purely a utility, though it conceded that “if I have a sense of humor, it’s strictly dry, record-based, and probably unintended.”

On Friday morning, stories on the site written by Walter included a report on a Fairbanks committee considering a rezone for 51 housing units, a federal task order awarded to an Idaho firm for snow removal at the Alcan border port, and a breakdown of state federal notices clearing 46 Alaska Native ancestors for return from museums.
The Browns are no strangers to unconventional tech setups or building tools off the beaten path.

After bootstrapping HasOffers in its early years , growing Tune into an $80 million business with over 300 employees, and taking on venture funding from firms like Accel Partners, the twins deliberately stepped away from the traditional startup treadmill in late 2018.

They relocated permanently to Valdez — a town of less than 4,000 residents known more for backcountry skiing than software development — where they set up Geeks in the Woods. Framed as an incubator operating far from Seattle in “the quiet space between code and wilderness,” the project builds software and infrastructure for a world where AI agents act as “first-class participants.”
Alaska News is just one piece of that experiment; their Valdez outpost also touches patent discovery, election-integrity research, agent-focused identity infrastructure, and AI-assisted music.

The Browns are part of a five-person founding team behind Alaska News. Alongside editor-in-chief Green, the project’s masthead includes Matt Larkin, a longtime Alaska pollster and political operative, and Grant Robinson, a former television reporter who serves as a spokesperson for Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy.
“Lee and I love being entrepreneurs and taking things from 0-to-1, turning crazy ideas into legit business concepts that can grow and scale,” Lucas Brown told GeekWire in 2019.

articles.title: From elections to board games: Washington’s secretary of state does double duty as a tabletop trade envoy
articles.author: Thomas Wilde
paras: If you explore the main expo hall during the Penny Arcade Expo, you can often find some interesting booths around the edges of the room. These can offer rare games, designer clothing, blind boxes of themed merch, and occasionally/inexplicably, unfiltered access to local Washington politicians.

Steve Hobbs has held the secretary of state position for Washington since 2021. Visitors to his booth during PAX, held over Labor Day weekend at the Seattle Convention Center, could meet Hobbs and spin a prize wheel, with rewards that included buttons, collectible pins featuring the office’s official mascot Finn, custom 20-sided dice with Finn on the 20 face, and free snacks.

This wasn’t Hobbs’ first time at PAX, but it was the first time I’d heard about a closed-doors event he’d hosted on the night before PAX. One of the local exhibitors mentioned that Hobbs’ office had held a networking event in Seattle on Thursday, Sept. 3, between local tabletop companies and an assortment of international game publishers.

That got me curious enough to schedule a short conversation with Hobbs on the third day of PAX. Once we sat down, however, I had to ask him the question that I’d heard from a lot of other attendees: what was he doing at PAX in the first place?

“It’s twofold,” Hobbs told me. “One, this is a great opportunity for me to reach out to the gaming companies here in the state of Washington and look for opportunities for them to go overseas, linking up some of these indie game developers with major publishers.”
He continued, “The rest of it is civic engagement. Just reminding people, hey, don’t forget to vote. Don’t forget to check your registration.”

Washington mails a ballot to every registered voter, who can return it by mail or at an official drop box. Hobbs was urging people to use the drop boxes, citing what he called “a low-key fight with the USPS.”

Washington and 24 other states sued in August to block a U.S. Postal Service rule requiring new barcodes on ballot envelopes, and the Supreme Court kept it from taking effect on Sept. 14, after this interview.
“Look, PAX is where all the young people are at, right?” Hobbs said. “This is a very diverse, young community, and this is where we need to engage people.”

The Thursday-night event was intended to help connect Washington’s homegrown board games industry with interested publishers and players in Japan, Poland and elsewhere. This could allow Washington-based designers to sell their products overseas, as well as potentially letting foreign partners export their own games to North America .

Washington doesn’t make quite as big a deal about it as one might expect, but it’s one of the biggest states in the U.S. for tabletop and board game design, if not the biggest. Local Washington studios range in size from Renton-based Wizards of the Coast to one-person indie creators who make card games as a hobby. Hobbs’ office estimated early last year that tabletop gaming in Washington is a $2 billion industry.

The Secretary of State’s Office is best known for its core duties of running elections and registering businesses, but state law also directs the secretary of state to develop a citizens’ exchange program promoting ties that “may result in increased tourism, business relationships, and trade.”

“So what we do is help these indie game developers get access to foreign markets by putting on these trade missions,” Hobbs said. “What we’ll do is provide the booth [at international gaming conferences, such as Game Market in Tokyo], which is the most expensive thing. We will also help them navigate through the federal grant process in order to mitigate some of the costs over there.”
His office then works its connections with the U.S. State Department and the host nation’s commerce department to set up meetings for the developers.
“We have really strong ties with the German and Japanese governments, and we actually get these people to do their pitches with the major publishers in Europe and Japan,” Hobbs said.

As an example of the initiative’s success, Hobbs pointed to Lethal Shadows, a Snohomish County business that specializes in premium tabletop miniatures. According to Hobbs, he’d helped Lethal Shadows partner up with a Lithuanian company . As a result, Lethal Shadows has moved from a garage to a warehouse and is hiring more employees.
That did raise the question of why Hobbs’ office wasn’t making equivalent inroads toward Washington’s significantly larger video game industry.

“It’s more of a lack of bandwidth,” Hobbs said. “We want to take baby steps. We didn’t want to take a big step into it. And frankly, I didn’t realize that it was important to go to these conventions. In Japan, Germany, and Poland, we’re seeing if there might be an opportunity to do the same thing on the digital side.”
Hobbs continued, “I believe trade must go two ways. We need to support each other.”

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: Quiet Zone in Kent
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: On August 24, 2026, Kent’s long-awaited Quiet Zone took effect along the BNSF Railway mainline through downtown. This designation, granted by the Federal Railroad Administration in June , no longer requires trains to sound their horn when approaching an at-grade crossing. Over the past 14 years, the City of Kent has worked to meet the necessary requirements to achieve a Quiet Zone. Recent infrastructure upgrades include building raised concrete medians, adding additional signs, and refreshing pavement markings. In a non-Quiet Zone area, all trains are required to sound their horn 15-20 seconds before each street crossing.

The BNSF mainline tracks are used by 38 passenger trains and many more freight trains every day. The frequent at-grade crossings in downtown Kent resulted in nearby residents hearing hundreds of train horns day and night. The Quiet Zone stretches between S 212th St and S 259th St. The following crossings are included:

As safety is still a top priority, train engineers are still allowed to sound the horn in emergency situations or as they deem necessary. While the Quiet Zone is officially in effect, it may take some time for nearby residents to hear a difference. One week after the change was implemented, the Kent Reporter noted that many trains were still using their horn at each crossing. I was in Kent earlier this week and each of the five trains (four Sounder, one Amtrak Cascades) I saw used their horn at each crossing.

articles.title: Traffic Safety Package Advances with Change Targeting Historic Districts
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: A three-bill package intended to improve Seattle's response to increasing rates of deaths and serious injuries on city streets was approved by City Council's transportation committee on Thursday. Introduced by committee chair Rob Saka and dubbed the SAFER Streets Act , the proposal largely empowers officials at the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) with explicit authority that they already have the ability to wield. But it also sets up future legislation around post-crash responses and safety upgrades to vehicles used by city contractors.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!
The committee approved a raft of amendments before a final vote, tweaks needed in part due to the package's rushed process to get advanced before the council's fall budget work.

Most of these were technical changes that didn't have big policy impacts, but one major amendment, put forward by Alexis Mercedes Rinck and approved on a 3-2 vote, proved contentious. It added a provision explicitly beefing up SDOT's authority to make changes to roadways within the city's historic districts, letting them sidestep an oftentimes lengthy historic board or commission approval process on certain safety-related changes.

Traffic safety advocates had been pushing for the city to receive that authority, in the wake of several high-profile incidents where city projects have met resistance at preservation boards in recent years. This spring, SDOT had to walk back a plan to deploy bike and scooter corrals across Pioneer Square to both keep sidewalks clear of micromobility devices but also to keep intersections clear of parked cars, a treatment known as intersection daylighting. Business owners in the district had raised concerns about aesthetics and lost parking, despite the original plan only involving the removal of one or two legal spots.

Under the amendment, "traffic control devices and spot design changes" in historic districts wouldn't be subject to landmark designation, nor would the city need to receive a Certificate of Approval (which can be appealed) to advance adjustments within Seattle's eight historic districts when it comes to that narrow range of adjustments.

"This amendment focuses on the Traffic Engineer's authority specifically over traffic control devices," Amanda Allen, a legislative analyst at the City, told councilmembers. "It does not include bollards, which may be of interest to folks, it is really focused on signs, signals, and markings."

Ahead of the vote, advocates of historic districts across the city showed up to testify at city hall in opposition to the change. Comments regarding Pioneer Square and Pike Place were the most prevalent, but they also included concerns about Ballard Avenue and Chinatown-International District.

"We believe safety and preservation are not in conflict, and they have not been historically," Alliance for Pioneer Square Executive Director Lisa Howard said during public comment, suggesting that this move had been put forward in response to the scooter corral incident alone. "We can make our streets safer without eliminating meaningful review in our historic districts."

Advocates have argued the corral debacle is far from an isolated incident. In 2024, SDOT was forced to negotiate with the Pioneer Square Preservation Board over a two-block protected bike connection along Yesler Way between Occidental Avenue and Western Avenue, the only direct bike lane planned between the waterfront and central downtown. An initial presentation noted construction could have started as soon as July of that year, but the department was forced to come back for a second meeting in the fall, after potential issues were raised about driver access to I-5 from the neighborhood.
In the end, the connection did not go in until early 2026, and with a last-minute adjustment to retain a potentially dangerous left turn in response to "community feedback."

Inside Pike Place Market, this adjustment would likely not give SDOT unilateral authority to keep vehicle traffic out of the Market, in the wake of recent historical commission approval of three-day "soft closures" every week through the winter, ramping down a successful Pike Place pedestrianization pilot. But it would give the department more tools than it has currently.
In putting forward her amendment, Rinck expressed support for the city's historic districts, but spelled out the need to elevate safety issues above other changes within those districts.

"I hope we can agree that some things are just too important to subject to the Seattle Process, and I believe traffic safety meets that bar," Rinck said. "I've been told this amendment goes too far, but I dare to say the city has not gone far enough when it comes to preventing traffic deaths and injuries. So I hope people hear today that my bringing this amendment forward is in response to the calls for decisive action that I've heard from families who have lost loved ones on our streets, our transit advocates, and everyone who has had too close of a call."

While Rinck's amendment did pass, there are outstanding questions about whether it is fully implementable as written. It does not make any changes to the section of city code directly governing historic districts, and it would take a completely different bill with a different subject to make those updates. In addition, District 2 Councilmember Eddie Lin suggested an additional carveout might be necessary for Chinatown-International District, which was included on a list of the 11 most endangered historic places in the U.S. in 2023.
But Lin, along with amendment co-sponsor Dionne Foster, voted to give the amendment the green light for now.

"I do think there's a way to to do historic preservation and achieve public safety, but I do think at the end of the day, the authority needs to lie with with who is responsible, and that is, in my opinion, the traffic engineer," Lin said. "The traffic engineer should, whenever possible, take into consideration any recommendations and feedback so that it's consistent with the historic preservation. At the end of the day, the traffic engineer is responsible for traffic safety, and we have seen in in polling, how traffic safety in recent years has been the number one public safety concern, and there's good reason behind that."

Bob Kettle, who represents the district that includes Pike Place Market, raised issues with the process to review the amendment, as well as a lack of outreach to the specific districts that would be impacted in voting against the amendment.

"As it relates to the legislative process, I am a little bit astonished that we're looking at an amendment that was not seen by our in-house legal counsel until this morning. There was issues in the city attorney's office with its review. There was no consideration of the state pieces, state law, and the like," Kettle said. "And as it relates to stakeholdering, I don't think obviously – Pike Place Market wasn't stakeholdered, Pioneer Square wasn't stakeholdered. I tend to doubt that Chinatown International District was stakeholdered on this."

Saka, who also voted no, said that this potential tweak had come up during the development of the overall package, and had been suggested directly by SDOT as a potential reform. But he did state that he could support a more narrowly tailored amendment that didn't treat all of the eight historic districts the same.

"I declined to accept it for a reason," Saka said. "I do appreciate the the intent [or] spirit here behind this, and we need to have tough policy conversations and be willing to do things up to and including this at some point, I just don't think we've done the the work and stakeholdering to do that. I know my constituents in Pioneer Square don't like this, even though I know they strongly support safety."

It is likely that the proposal sees some modifications ahead of a vote of the full council set for mid-October, including potential changes that involve notification of the historic boards on projects that may no longer require direct approval.

"It's critical that we have clarity around the role of the City Traffic Engineer and their authority to make decisions around safety, so that we can work towards the goals that we all share when it comes to traffic safety, public safety, and Vision Zero," Dionne Foster said. "I intend to bring an amendment to full council that commits SDOT to providing notification to the historic boards of significant changes to traffic control devices within the historic districts. I believe in this way we can ensure that we have clarity on the decision making as well as clarity on the information sharing."

articles.title: Deconstruction Is a Key Frontier for Climate Action in Seattle
articles.author: Syris Valentine
paras: Aaron Blanchard recalls taking a tour through the broken-open guts of a building across from the downtown ferry terminal with a crew from Dixon Demolition as they prepared to take the building down. Crawling through holes in the walls to move from section to section, he was struck by all the immense, exposed timbers that framed and supported the structure.

“Normally, there’s all this drywall,” Blanchard said. “There’s all this other stuff you’ve got to deal with.” But in that building, it was nothing but lumber, and Blanchard wanted to make sure none of it went to the landfill.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

[Note: This article is a follow up to a three-part series on Seattle’s Climate Action Plan. Part One: The history of climate action in Seattle . Part Two: The current state of climate action in Seattle . Part Three: Climate action for a resilient Seattle .]

Salvage assessments like that are required in Seattle before any building comes down or undergoes a substantial alteration. As director of operations and part-owner of Earthwise Architectural Salvage — a company with 35 years in the salvaging business — Blanchard has supported plenty of these assessments, looking for anything worth saving that he can either resell as is or remanufacture for sale. Cabinets, doors, windows, and the like are all that’s worth prying out of most prospective demolitions for Earthwise. Other than that, it’s just loads of drywall and two-by-four lumber.

But when Blanchard walked through this particular building along Alaskan Way, he saw little that wasn’t worth saving. He turned to the demolition contractor and said: “You guys know this is going to be a deconstruction, right? You’re gonna save so much of this wood, and we’re gonna buy it from you.”

To dangle an extra carrot, Blanchard told them about Seattle Public Utilities’ (SPU’s) deconstruction incentive , which provides contractors with $6,000 per commercial project when the building is taken down board by board and beam by beam. That incentive typically only covers a slim, single digit percentage of a project’s cost, but deconstruction offers its own ways for contractors to cut costs and recoup expenses. Crews don’t need to pay the tonnage fee of shipping waste to the landfill, and they can get some additional cash back when they sell salvaged materials to a company like Earthwise.

This incentive is one of several bids on the part of SPU to promote a circular economy in Seattle. Creating pathways that divert materials from the landfill and instead cycle through the economy in different forms has recently gained increased attention inside the City. Late last year, the Office of Sustainability and Environment (OSE) began the process to revamp the citywide climate action plan. That effort means more than simply updating goals and timelines; they’re incorporating new areas of focus into the plan as well. They presented the action areas for public discussion during a July forum . One area looked squarely at how the City can “reuse more, waste less.”

The motivation for this comes from a simple fact that many within the climate sphere used to overlook. “Climate change is a product not only of greenhouse gas emissions, but the amount of economic activity,” Deric Gruen, a co-founder of the nonprofit Peoples Economy Lab, told The Urbanist

If people repair, reuse, repurpose, and even simply share more , then they not only prevent waste from piling up in landfills already nearing capacity , they also reduce the need to open up more minelands, log more forests, or extract more fossil fuels with all the environmental damages they bring.

In Seattle, circularity gained steam after a 2023 exercise in which OSE and SPU partnered together to consider how the picture of Seattle’s emissions changes when we look beyond transportation, buildings, and municipal waste alone to factor in how eating habits, purchasing patterns, travel plans, and household activities shape global warming, even when the associated carbon enters the atmosphere far outside city limits. This approach is called a consumption-based emissions inventory .

SPU wanted to understand how consumption in Seattle affected the city’s climate footprint and “how our work around waste prevention and changing the way that we think about materials can support the broader global emissions reduction efforts,” said SPU’s circular economy policy advisor Ashima Sukhdev.
“It totally shifts the strategy,” Gruen said. “A consumption-based inventory asks, how are we meeting our needs and what’s our responsibility for that whole supply chain?”

This requires City officials to think about what can be done to lessen the imprint left on the environment by every aspect of a resident’s life. Much of the work that goes into the circular economy thinks about all the things that people engage with and dispose of on a daily basis: food, clothes, dishware, and the like. For instance, since 2022, SPU has led the Reuse Seattle partnership that aims to replace single-use containers across Seattle’s cafes, restaurants, and event venues with reusable alternatives .

This summer, SPU and the Office of Economic Development also helped Seattle Reconomy to open the Reuse Commons in Lake City where nonprofits, businesses, and community organizations can host events, provide mutual support, and work under one roof to make it easy as possible for people in the community to engage with the circular economy. In its final form, the commons would operate as a sort of mall.

“Imagine somebody comes into the reuse commons, drops off their kids' goods, their bike, their tools, their furniture. We take that, we organize it and redistribute it,” Josh Epstein, the executive director of Seattle Reconomy, told The Urbanist . “And on the other side of the reuse commons is our storefront where we're selling fixed, upcycled furniture and art and bikes and tools.”
The commons would also provide a new space for Reconomy’s central offering: sharing libraries where members can borrow tools, dishware, basic appliances, and other common goods.

Epstein believes the Reuse Commons represents a huge opportunity for residents of Lake City and North Seattle, and it also could provide a model for something that Seattle Reconomy and partners like the Furniture Repair Bank could recreate in South Seattle .

Projects like these with a focus on consumer goods can help, but advocates like Dave Bennink see the biggest potential for reducing waste and society’s burden on the environment as lying in the built environment, in particular by thinking about construction and demolition in new ways—by thinking about deconstruction.

The average American generates 4.9 pounds of trash per day , adding up to around 141,000 pounds in a lifetime. It’s a staggering number that numerous organizations in the city , state , and country are working to drive down. But as Bennink, the director of the Building Deconstruction Institute, pointed out in a conversation with The Urbanist , the average home in America weighs between 80,000 and 160,000 pounds . So, demolishing a home is a great way to speed-run the waste budget of your life.

“It doesn't matter how many bottles you recycle and how many newspapers you recycle,” said Bennink, “if you choose to demolish your building, then you have wasted an entire lifetime's worth of materials.” To solve the issue, his company has helped prove out a workable alternative: “We don't demolish [buildings]. We disassemble them.”

As a national expert in deconstruction, Bennink has helped train contractors across 45 states, five provinces, and nine countries, and he has advised at least 22 municipalities — including Portland, Seattle, and King County — considering policies and programs to grow local deconstruction industries. The collective impact he and his team have accomplished since Bennink started this work in 1993 has been immense: Across more than 5,000 projects, Bennink’s team has diverted more than 100 million pounds from the landfill and reclaimed wood and lumber equivalent to 10,000 acres of standing forest. But his work advising policies and helping entrepreneurs start their own circular businesses has the potential to multiply that impact.

Of course, it’s all well and good to reclaim wood, but the real impact comes when that wood is reused, both Bennink and Blanchard pointed out. For someone like Bennink who has been in the business for decades and helped foster an ecosystem around him of people bought into reclaiming and reusing lumber, it’s easy enough to find a new building to take whatever is extracted from an old one.
“If we remove some wood flooring from one home,” Bennink said, “then we have someone in our group of businesses now that will reinstall it in somebody else's home.”

But creating that kind of ecosystem requires a lot of capacity that many contractors may not have. “If your model is selling the wood to make up the difference between demolition and deconstruction,” Blanchard said, “well, now you also have to have a lumber company.”

That’s why the City of Seattle, with the support of a $4 million grant from the Environmental Protection Agency, partnered with Earthwise to open a new Salvage Lumber Warehouse in SoDo earlier this year . It provides a simple destination for contractors to sell what wood they save, and then it’s up to Earthwise to find a customer for it. Most of those customers are homeowners and business owners working on smaller projects.

With all the benefits that come from deconstruction, some environmentalists have argued it should be a requirement, and some cities have taken the plunge with their own versions of such mandates . In 2016, Portland became the first city in the nation to establish an ordinance requiring deconstruction, specifically on all buildings built before 1940.

Since then, cities like Boulder, Colorado; Palo Alto, California; San Antonio, Texas; and Baltimore, Maryland, have instituted their own versions of such an ordinance. In contrast, Seattle still relies on an incentive, which has been used sparingly thus far. Just 45 projects have used that incentive since it launched, according to SPU. In that same time, SPU has issued 750 demolition permits for single family homes alone.

While having just 6% of homes deconstructed instead of demolished feels low given the potential impact that this can bring, Blanchard pointed out that not every building has materials that are worth saving, which can make an ordinance with mandatory salvage rates tricky to implement. It could easily mean you’re saving heaps of wood that no one wants to buy, so they just end up languishing in a warehouse instead of the landfill.
“You need to balance the new supply that you will be creating of reclaimed materials with a new demand,” Bennink added.

Integrating reclaimed lumber into other projects, whether new construction or renovation, is where the real environmental benefits of this practice shows up. According to one study , when reclaimed wood is used in a project instead of virgin timber, the net demand for energy is 13 times lower and the total emissions are five times lower as well.

Ensuring there is demand for those materials, however, means that a city must ease its way into any sort of mandate. That’s why when Portland was first considering its ordinance, Bennink recommended they start with an incentive. An incentive period gives all parties involved in the built environment time to understand what deconstruction means for properties around the city and what it takes to be successful in that project. More importantly, it helps the industry to levelize costs and timing with traditional demolitions.

Because deconstruction can require more labor power and specialized skills, some firms feel justified in charging extra to dismantle a building in that way — even when they have opportunities to cut other costs and gain additional incomes. But Bennink’s vision is for deconstruction costs to be less than traditional demolition.
“We don't want it to cost more,” he said. “We don't want it to take more time. We don't want to adversely affect people's projects.”

Bennink has spent three decades refining his methods to ensure deconstruction can be done economically, and when he trains local workforces, as he has done in Portland and King County, he tries to impart those skills onto others. When The Urbanist spoke with Bennink, he was in the middle of taking apart a pole barn.
“We were half the price of demolition,” he said. “For other buildings, we might be 25% more than the price of demolition, and on lots of buildings we are equal to the price.”

So with a relatively new deconstruction trade emerging in Seattle, costs might currently be higher than demolition in many cases, but if the City increases use of its incentive or begins to transition to a mandate on some projects, those cost disparities should narrow in the coming years. Boosting the use of deconstruction and salvage across the city’s building stock could end up being an important part of Seattle’s climate strategy, and potentially the City’s upcoming update to its climate action plan.

articles.title: Riders sound off on fare gates coming to Capitol Hill Station
articles.author: AGPhoto
paras: Fare gates are coming to Capitol Hill Station, and the neighborhood has feelings about it.

As CHS reported last month , the Sound Transit board voted to move forward with an $87 million pilot to install fare gates at 14 stations on the 1 and 2 Lines, Capitol Hill included. Gates aren’t expected to show up at Broadway and John until 2029 or 2030, but the vote is a real shift for an agency that has run Link as an open, proof-of-payment system since 2009.

The reason: systemwide farebox recovery has been running around 11% to 14%, far short of Sound Transit’s 40% goal. Fare evasion hit roughly 45% of riders in 2023 before gaining with Fare Ambassadors on board; the agency projects it’ll still sit near 25% by 2029, well above the 2.4% rate seen before the pandemic. Capitol Hill Station itself sees about 11,000 boardings a day, some 40% above pre-pandemic levels.
CHS asked a few riders at the station what they think.

Matt is on board: “I’m pro. I’m a fan of fare gates,” though he doubts gates move much revenue on their own. Dee pointed to peer cities: “San Francisco, New York, Tokyo. They all have fare gates.” For riders who already pay, Dee said, nothing changes: “How would it impact you? Not at all.”

Steven called gates “probably the most straightforward way” to handle evasion. David , who pays every month on a senior card, noted gated platforms are standard elsewhere too, like Vancouver: “It’s not like some radical departure.” Lily saw it as a fit for high-traffic, tourist-heavy stops like Capitol Hill: “It’s not the only way, but I think it is one way to do it.”

Mia called the plan “a waste of money,” pointing to New York as a cautionary tale on maintenance costs, and would rather see subsidized ORCA cards. Dana was blunter: “Unnecessary spending… people don’t want to pay if they’re not going to pay, and maybe they can’t pay.”

Troy favors the trust system, though he admits the numbers give him pause: “If a third of the people aren’t paying, that’s a high number.” Jack wants proof before Sound Transit spends $87 million: “I don’t see a lot of crime in the system here, so I don’t know if that’s a solution without a problem.”

Madeline , who says she doesn’t always pay, worries about access: “A lot of people will lose access to transit, and it’s important for everybody to have.” Sally tied the gates to the station’s role as informal shelter space: “If you close this off, where are those people going?” Angela reframed the whole debate: “It shouldn’t be about the gates. It should be about what is the solution so that everybody can get where they need to go.”

Several riders said light rail should just be free. Others who support gates called that unrealistic. Sally pointed to Boston’s model, where wealthier riders effectively subsidized the rest. “You have to weigh the pros and cons.”

Sound Transit’s financial modeling projects the $87 million investment will reach a break-even point within two to three years of rollout. By launching the pilot with the 14 enclosed, high-volume stations like Capitol Hill rather than attempting a costlier systemwide buildout, Sound Transit expects to capture roughly 85% of overall ridership. Addressing affordability, transit officials says that light rail isn’t designed to be self-sustaining — fares are only budgeted to cover 22% of day-to-day operating costs, with local taxes subsidizing the rest alongside discount programs like ORCA LIFT aimed at keeping fares accessible.

Design alone is budgeted at $6 million of the $87 million total, and nothing physical changes at Broadway and John for years. For now, riders at Broadway and John will keep doing what they’ve always done: tap in, or don’t, and hope the ambassadors are in a forgiving mood.

articles.title: Seattle Is Poised to Ban Supermarket Algorithmic Price Discrimination
articles.author: Guy Oron
paras: This coming Tuesday, in an effort to crack down on price gouging and discrimination, the Seattle City Council will vote on a bill prohibiting large grocery store companies from using customer personal information to customize prices and discounts.

Proposed by Mayor Katie Wilson and Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck, the legislation will require grocery stores with more than 20 locations worldwide to stop using personal data to set individualized prices and discounts. It would also apply to third party delivery apps such as Instacart, as well as mixed-used stores like Target.

The idea that grocery companies are charging different people different prices based on their past purchases sounds like a futuristic dystopia. But it’s not far off. The practice isn’t in brick and mortar stores yet, but it’s a widespread reality for online shopping. And they’ve already been hoarding your data for years.

Back in 2019, the marketing arm of Kroger, the supermarket giant that owns QFC and Fred Meyer, boasted about collecting more than 2,000 data points on customers using past purchasing history and information bought from data brokers. That data will feed the new pricing algorithms.

Those algorithms are designed to estimate a customer’s purchasing power and how willing they might be to pay more. As part of a Consumer Reports study last year, 39 volunteers loaded up virtual Instacart baskets of products from a Seattle Safeway store. They received a range of prices from $114 to $124 for the exact same goods. That study estimated that this type of price manipulation, if applied to a family of four, could result in cost differences as high as $1,200 a year.

While currently algorithmic pricing is mainly limited to online shopping and loyalty apps, it’s right around the corner for brick-and-mortar stores with the introduction of electronic price labels , which allow stores to instantly change prices of goods. The city council ordinance will require these labels to be the same for different customers.

Uptown QFC cashier and florist Kristen Wilder told The Stranger that Kroger already started rolling out these electronic labels at her store in July. She says customers already hate that they can only access most coupons through an app which collects their data, and she’s worried about the impact of the new labels if the bill doesn’t pass. Wilder’s union, UFCW 3000, has been a key backer of the legislation.

Kerem Levitas, a senior policy advisor in Mayor Wilson’s office says Seattle would be the first city to enact a ban on grocery algorithmic price discrimination, though Portland and New York City are already working on similar legislation. This wouldn’t be entirely novel. Maryland, New Jersey, and Connecticut have already passed similar statewide regulations. The City’s legislation is partially based on a similar statewide bill introduced this year that did not pass.

Washington People’s Privacy founder Maya Morales believes the Seattle bill could be the most comprehensive. It doesn’t allow exemptions for individualized discounts, which can be used to get around fair pricing rules.

“What happens is people are offered these individualized discounts, but often they’ve used a deceptive pricing model and a deceptive discount model to actually end up with customers paying more,” Morales said. So even if the prices are the same, allowing customized coupons would still allow companies to discriminate.

Under the ordinance, large grocery store companies will have to offer discounts based on equal criteria. So, if you get a buy-one-get-one-free deal for accruing a certain amount of loyalty points, other customers must also receive the same deal. Discounts based on certain allowable characteristics—deals for seniors, for veterans—would still be allowed, as long as everyone in that category receives it.

Because company algorithms are proprietary, it’s hard for independent auditors to read the source code and see if they are violating civil rights laws. Morales argues that the only way to prevent pricing discrimination based on race or other protected classes is by banning individualized pricing altogether.

Predictably, big grocers are mad. Grocery store lobby groups are flooding city council with testimony asking for a personalized discounts loophole. The Northwest Grocery Retail Association even employed a mass texting service to ask Seattleites to send letters to the council. The form email is definitely not astroturfed: “Please amend the ordinance to make the rules clear: don’t use my information to charge me more, but don’t prevent it from being used to help me save.”
The Northwest Grocery Retail Association did not respond to a request for comment.

Lead sponsor Rinck says she hasn’t any constituents in favor of having their data used to get personalized discounts. In fact, she said the vast majority of real-life people who are showing up at public comment support the legislation.

“When I talk to people, they’ve expressed to me a lot of discomfort with how their data is now being used and how it could be used against them,” Rinck said. “The price of groceries should be based on the product, not on who the shopper is or what an algorithm thinks they will pay.”
